transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start: 04:00 PM PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moore (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Tom Garcia (ClearPath Eng Lead), Maya Chen (CTO), Jordan Lee (SRE)

Summary:
Short demo showing hosted Chat/Text generation basics: streaming vs sync, common parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop), retry/backoff pattern and idempotency, and a quick tour of Console and Optimize suggestions for cost/perf. Q&A on security and data residency.

Topics covered:
- Quick qualification: latency & cost targets, regulatory concerns, current stack (GCP), traffic patterns
- Streaming behavior and chunk correlation (resume, partial tokens)
- Parameter tuning for deterministic vs creative responses (temp/top_p/seeding)
- Retry semantics, idempotency tokens, exponential backoff, distinguishing client vs server errors
- Console: per-route cost breakdown, token-level latency, rollout/canary settings
- Optimize: batching recommendations, quantization suggestions, KV/prefix cache notes

Transcript body:
[00:00:02] Alex: okay, um hi everyone thanks for joining. alex moore here from Redwood, i'm the deal owner. priya my se will run the demo portion, quick intro from you?
[00:00:10] Priya: hey all, priya shah, infra and runtime, i'll show a sandbox chat gen walk through, streaming and retry examples.
[00:00:18] Tom: thanks, tom garcia here, eng lead on the payments chatbot project. maya and jordan are on to listen for security and infra questions.
[00:00:25] Maya: hi.
[00:00:26] Jordan: hey team.
[00:00:28] Alex: cool, quick agenda — 1) quick fit questions, 2) demo streaming + params, 3) retry playbook, 4) console/optimize highlights, 5) q&a and next steps. sound good?
[00:00:38] Tom: yep. let's dive.

[00:01:05] Alex: first, can you share the SLOs — what's acceptable p95 / p99 latency for your live chat flows and rough volume?
[00:01:14] Tom: baseline goal is p95 < 400ms for short responses (few tokens), p99 < 1s if possible. traffic initially 30 RPS peak but spiky during checkout events maybe 150 RPS bursts.
[00:01:28] Maya: also important, we have SOC2 and need audit logs, and data-at-rest encryption with our KMS.
[00:01:35] Alex: ok noted — Redwood hosted supports SOC2, and we integrate with external KMS for private deployments; hosted keeps logs but we can show retention.

[00:02:00] Priya: alright demo — i'll open the sandbox in the console, but first quick architecture note: our hosted chat endpoint streams chunks as partial tokens in event-stream, clients should be prepared to handle incremental events and reassembly. we send chunk_metadata: sequence_id, request_id, and partial_is_final flags so you can correlate. (slight mispronunciation: we call it the 'conversational stream' but sometimes the transcript shows 'conversion stream')
[00:02:28] Priya: showing code now — simple curl to hit /v1/chat/stream with header x-request-id and x-idempotency-key. we highly recommend idempotency keys for create-like calls so retries from clients don't double-charge or double-generate.
[00:02:45] [00:02:46] Tom: is the idempotency keyed only for sync or does it apply to streamed responses too?
[00:02:52] Priya: good q — it applies for both, the idempotency token is tied to the request object; for streaming we will still return the same stream result if the upstream idempotency is matched, but note if you stream partials and the connection drops, a resumed request with the same idempotency will start a fresh stream with the same deterministic output only if you used deterministic params (temp 0 or seeded). otherwise results can vary.

[00:03:30] Priya: quick param primer — temperature (0-1+): 0 is deterministic, 0.7 is creative. top_p for nucleus sampling; max_tokens controls truncation. stop sequences are important for chat turn boundaries — we recommend explicit stop tokens at the end of assistant replies to avoid token leakage into user instructions. we show an example with temperature 0.2 and a top_p 0.9 for pragmatic answers.
[00:04:05] Jordan: for our use case we need deterministic for receipts and creative for marketing copy in other flows — can we route different flows to different model configs?
[00:04:12] Priya: yep — you can pin per-route defaults in Console, or set them client-side per request. Console also supports rollouts so you can A/B config changes.

[00:04:45] [00:04:47] Priya: streaming semantics — two failure classes: connection-level (client disconnects) and server-side partials/errors. for client disconnects, we provide resume tokens up to a small window (we keep recent KV prefixes for warm resumes). but remember resume is not magic — if you resume after longer than cache window, the runtime may re-evaluate and you could see divergent outputs unless deterministic params used.
[00:05:15] Tom: what's that cache window roughly?
[00:05:18] Priya: currently ~12–20s for prefix resume in hosted; for Dedicated we can tune that with KV cache size. that's part of the Optimize recommendations if you need longer windows. (slight stutter) excuse me, we can also do local client-side reconnection logic and request re-issue with idempotency keys.

[00:05:45] Priya: moving to retries — pattern we suggest: classify errors: 4xx client errors -> don't retry; 429/503 -> retry with jittered exponential backoff; 500/502/504 -> retry with backoff but monitor for repeated server-side failures. include a max attempt count (3 by default) and use idempotency keys for safe retries.
[00:06:10] Maya: do you support guidance for backoff windows and client libraries?
[00:06:13] Alex: yes, our SDKs include built-in retry policies you can configure; and in Console we show per-route error rates so you can adapt timeouts. Priya will share the sample client code.

[00:06:45] [00:06:46] Priya: quick live curl demo — sending a streaming call. (typing noises) we set temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120, stop sequence ['\nUSER:'] so assistant stops on user marker. streaming starts: we get events with chunk 1/6, chunk 2/6 etc. show how the client can render partials and commit final when partial_is_final true.
[00:07:20] Priya: small gotcha: if your client double-opens a stream (retry during a very slow connection) without idempotency, you may see two streams and duplicated output. recommend: 1) open single stream per request, 2) use idempotency, 3) detect and dedupe on request_id on your side.

[00:07:50] Tom: do you include token-delimited timing to measure per-token latency in the stream?
[00:07:55] Priya: yes — Console can surface token-level latency and per-token timing in traces. you can export traces to your tracing system via open telemetry hooks.

[00:08:20] [00:08:22] Priya: now short section on params to control cost — shorter max_tokens saves cost; use stop sequences aggressively so model doesn't hallucinate or continue longer. also prefix caching is big: if many requests share the same starter prompts (system + user context that is identical for many users), caching that KV saves compute. Optimize will recommend prefix caching and batching heuristics based on your traffic patterns.
[00:08:50] Jordan: our prompts include customer info that we can't send to hosted — data residency concern. what are options?
[00:08:57] Alex: two options typically: 1) hosted with retention controls and contractual commitments (we hold minimal logs and can offer short retention), or 2) Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) where you control KMS and network. We can scope this for POC.

[00:09:30] Priya: back to retries — we also recommend idempotent primitives for non-chat endpoints (embeddings, rerank), but chat is a little trickier. for chat flows, if determinism is required, set temperature to 0 and pin seed (we expose a seed param for many models) so idempotent retries yield the same text. otherwise you should treat repeated attempts as new generations.

[00:10:05] Priya: i'll now show Console: route config page. here's per-route default params, traffic split, and per-model latency/cost heatmap. notice the Optimize suggestion pane — it shows batching size recommendations and a quantization suggestion for a model variant (int8) to save ~40% on per-token cost at a small quality delta. (transcription misreads 'quantization' as 'quantity zation' for a moment)
[00:10:40] Tom: how do you measure quality delta? we need to ensure receipts remain perfect.
[00:10:44] Priya: Optimize runs evals on your prompt sets or our reference evals. it will show regression metrics against your golden examples; we can set alert thresholds for regressions. for receipts and sensitive flows, we generally recommend non-quantized or careful human-in-the-loop review.

[00:11:20] [00:11:22] Priya: another console feature — rollout rules: you can do canary with 5% traffic, monitor latency and error rate windows, and auto-fallback if thresholds exceeded. that helps guard against new model variants causing regressions.

[00:12:00] Maya: curious about auth and SSO — do you support SAML for console access?
[00:12:05] Alex: yes SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC and audit logs are supported. we'll include our security brief with SOC2/ISO artifacts.

[00:12:28] Priya: demoing a failure scenario — we artificially cause a server 503. client gets 503 mid-stream. pattern: client should capture the request_id and idempotency key, run backoff, and re-issue if safe. if user-facing, show partial fallback content like 'Sorry, we're having trouble, retrying' and then attempt automatic retry with exponential backoff up to 3 tries.
[00:13:05] Tom: how are streaming partials recovered? suppose we received chunk 1-3 then 503, do we resume or re-gen?
[00:13:12] Priya: short answer: resume if within the resume window and you have resume token; otherwise re-gen. resumed stream may skip token overlap handling so clients should be prepared to dedupe last few tokens or use a finalization handshake to confirm last committed token index.

[00:13:50] [00:13:52] Priya: performance tuning tips — increase concurrency but be mindful of batching: large batch sizes improve throughput cost but add latency. for low-latency UX we prefer small batches or even single-request paths. Console Optimize will recommend batch sizes per route based on sequence length distribution.
[00:14:20] Jordan: do you provide per-API rate limits or customer-specific quotas?
[00:14:24] Alex: yes rate limits and quotas are configurable per-account. Dedicated includes guaranteed capacity pools for predictable throughput.

[00:14:50] Priya: now a quick walkthrough of sample SDK calls — JavaScript and Go examples use automatic retries with jitter, idempotency by default for non-streamed calls; for streaming we show a streaming client that emits events and reassembles text. we'll share the repo link.

[00:15:30] [00:15:32] Priya: let's run a live prompt from your prompts — Tom, can you share a short example?
[00:15:38] Tom: sure: 'You are the payments assistant, summarize the last transaction and flag suspicious items.' keep it short.
[00:15:45] Priya: sending with temp 0.2 and stop sequence '\nUSER:' — streaming result comes back, partials shown, final commit. shows quick p95 ~320ms for this short reply.
[00:16:05] Tom: nice.

[00:16:20] Maya: any recommended metric thresholds for switching to Dedicated? we care about consistent p99.
[00:16:28] Alex: rule of thumb — if you need consistent multi-region or guaranteed latency under heavy burst with predictable SLA, Dedicated is better. for pilot and early phases hosted is usually fine. we can model costs based on your projected RPS and token sizes.

[00:17:05] Priya: notes on logs and PII — we provide request-level audit logs and you can opt to disable retention for hosted; for strict PII rules, Private with customer-managed KMS is typical. We'll include a short security comparison doc.

[00:17:40] [00:17:42] Tom: what about debugging streams — can we replay traces?
[00:17:45] Priya: yes trace export, and in Console you can view recent streams with per-chunk timestamps. retention window depends on plan.

[00:18:15] Priya: quick troubleshooting mini-checklist: 1) network timeouts: increase socket timeout to 90s, 2) idempotency: include keys, 3) maintain request-level logs with request_id, 4) tune batching in Optimize, 5) pin deterministic params for reproducible retries.

[00:18:50] Maya: good checklist.

[00:19:10] [00:19:12] Alex: ok wrapping up momentarily — any other blockers for a pilot?
[00:19:18] Tom: our main blockers: security docs + KMS options, cost estimate for pilot, and a simple bench harness to run our prompts against Redwood hosted.
[00:19:28] Alex: we'll provide those. Priya will share a bench script and console recording.

[00:19:45] [00:19:47] Priya: demo end — now q&a. Jordan you had a nitty-gritty infra question?
[00:19:52] Jordan: yeah, how do you handle abrupt node restarts on dedicated? will in-flight streams be lost?
[00:19:58] Priya: in that event, Dedicated keeps warm replicas and the router can failover; in-flight streams may be interrupted, hence we recommend client-side retries with idempotency and can optionally enable cross-node prefix persistence for longer resume windows.

[00:20:30] Tom: If we hit a 503 spike during checkout, can traffic fallback to smaller cheaper model automatically?
[00:20:36] Alex: yes you can set routing policies: fallback to a cheaper model variant or regionally lower-latency model, and Console rollouts let you configure fallback thresholds. be careful on quality regressions for sensitive flows like receipts.

[00:21:10] [00:21:12] Priya: one more practical thing: sequence length and tokenization — measure your average token count per prompt+reply; it matters for batching and choose models with good long context support if you carry conversation state.

[00:21:45] Maya: do you provide a prebuilt bench harness or should we adapt ours?
[00:21:48] Priya: we'll send a simple Node/Go bench script that hits stream and sync endpoints and collects p95/p99, token counts, and cost per 1k tokens. it's in the repo link we'll share.

[00:22:20] Alex: ok let's recap — next steps: Alex sends pricing and pilot terms; Priya sends console recording, bench harness, and cURL samples; customer sends prompts and SLOs; schedule POC kickoff next week.

[00:22:40] Tom: sounds good. thanks.
[00:22:45] Maya: thanks everyone.
[00:22:46] Jordan: appreciate it.

[00:23:00] (meeting closed, recording stopped)
